Triggers.value: Visible injuries or wounds on others

Threat.value: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I wake during the night to check whether I am safe

Memory.value: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

Negative Appraisals.value: You can never know who will harm you
I can't trust that I will do the right thing
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette:
Mariana was twenty-four when she was abducted from her apartment and held for three days by a trafficking ring. During that time she was tortured-beaten, burned, and systematically humiliated. One of her captors was a woman who would enter the concrete room alone, mock her, and inflict pain while Mariana lay bound on a mattress, her own blood and bruises visible, with no way out. That specific image-the female guard, the sight of her wounds, the total entrapment-became the fixed point around which everything else revolved.

After her rescue, Mariana returned to her job as an HVAC technician. She had always been good with her hands, and the work paid the bills. But within weeks she found herself scanning every room before she stepped into it. At night she checked her apartment door three times before sleeping and would wake, heart pounding, to verify the locks again. A sudden bang from a dropped tool made her flinch so hard her coworkers noticed. She began to believe that she could never know who would harm her next-that anyone, even a woman, might be a threat. This fear of harm kept her alert, and the alertness itself confirmed that she was no longer safe anywhere, that something in her was permanently broken.

The memory of the female tormentor intruded unpredictably, often when Mariana least expected it. She would be driving home and suddenly feel the shame of that powerless moment, as if the event were happening to someone else, a stranger whose degradation she could only watch. The shame was overwhelming, forcing her to pull over and breathe. The more she believed she had permanently changed, the more alien and shameful the memory felt-it seemed to belong to a person she no longer recognized. And each time the memory crashed in, her threat level spiked again. She would start checking her rearview mirror for followers, then check locks once more when she got home.

At work, triggers accumulated. A female client alone in a house made Mariana's stomach clench; she began avoiding assignments where a woman would be home by herself, making excuses to her dispatcher. Seeing a visible injury on a coworker-a cut, a bruise-sent her adrenaline soaring; she would stare at it and then quickly look away, her startle response primed. She found herself trapped in hallways or small boiler rooms and her breath would quicken, because having no options reminded her of the cell. These triggers created a constant undercurrent of threat that eroded her concentration. She started checking doors and windows at client sites, even when there was no reason. Her hypervigilance also made her see triggers everywhere: a woman walking toward her on the street became a potential captor, a Band-Aid on a child's arm became a sign of violence.

The more Mariana checked and started, the more she doubted herself. I can't trust that I'll do the right thing, she thought after fumbling a simple repair because she was too busy scanning the room. Her fear of harm deepened: if she had to be this watchful, then danger must be real. The self-doubt and sense of permanent damage fed directly back into the memory-each flashback felt more shameful, more alien, because it fit the person she now believed herself to be: broken, unreliable, unsafe. And that memory, in turn, made her more sensitive to triggers. A woman's voice in the next room would immediately pull her back to the guard's mocking tone, and then the cycle tightened again.

A few months ago, her supervisor put her on a team working in a women's shelter-a project Mariana couldn't refuse without explanation. The first day she walked in and saw several women, some with visible injuries from domestic violence, and felt the walls close in. She nearly fled. That afternoon she called a mental health clinic. What brought her there was not a single symptom but the crushing weight of the loop: the memory, the fear, the checking, the avoidance, all feeding each other. She was terrified that she would not be able to keep her job, and even more terrified that she was permanently damaged and would never feel safe again. But she had come anyway, desperate for something to stop the spiral.
